title: Dinosaur and Fossil Detective Station
subtitle: How do we learn about dinosaurs from long ago?
coreQuestion: Dinosaurs are no longer around, so how do scientists know what they looked like and how they lived?
learningGoals: Know fossils and footprints are evidence about ancient life.
Begin distinguishing plant-eating, meat-eating, and defensive features.
misconceptions: All dinosaurs lived at the same time and place.
A fossil always means a complete skeleton.

hero.title: Dinosaur and Fossil Detective Station
hero.lead: Dinosaurs are far away in time, but fossils, footprints, and bones leave clues.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main scene is a child-friendly natural history exploration: fossils and footprints in the foreground, with a few gentle original dinosaurs in the background for feature observation.
hero.childPrompt: Pick up the little brush and find the clues dinosaurs left behind.
hero.parentPrompt: Focus on evidence, not monster battles or crowded dinosaur scenes.

classificationGroups.name: Plant-eating dinosaurs
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Some dinosaurs had long necks or mouths suited for eating leaves.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Focus on feature observation, not formal taxonomy.

classificationGroups.name: Meat-eating dinosaurs
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Some dinosaurs had sharp teeth and strong back legs.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Keep it gentle; do not dramatize hunting.

classificationGroups.name: Bodies for protection
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Horns, armor plates, and tail clubs may help protection.

classificationGroups.name: Evidence left behind
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Bones, footprints, and fossils tell us about the past.
classificationGroups.misconception: A fossil is a whole dinosaur.

representativeObjects.name: Long-neck dinosaur
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A long neck may help it reach high leaves.
representativeObjects.visualHint: long neck, big body, small head

representativeObjects.name: Horned dinosaur
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Horns and a frill may help protect it.
representativeObjects.visualHint: three horns and a large frill

representativeObjects.name: Armored dinosaur
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Armor-like plates and a tail club may help defense.

representativeObjects.name: Toothy meat-eater
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Sharp teeth and a strong body suggest it may hunt.
representativeObjects.visualHint: large head, sharp teeth, strong legs

representativeObjects.name: Flying ancient partner
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Pterosaurs were not dinosaurs, but often appear in dinosaur-age scenes.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking every flying ancient animal was a dinosaur.

representativeObjects.name: Fossil
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A fossil is an old trace of life kept in rock.
representativeObjects.visualHint: bone or shell mark in stone
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking fossils must be complete skeletons.

representativeObjects.name: Footprint
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Footprints can show where animals walked and how big their feet were.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking footprints are not fossil evidence.

mechanism.title: How do we learn like dinosaur detectives?

steps.childExplanation: Scientists look for bones, teeth, footprints, eggshells, and other clues.
Fossils are precious and must be cleaned slowly with small tools.
Teeth, legs, horns, and armor help us guess how it lived.
Many clues together help imagine the animal and its environment.
New fossils can change scientific ideas.
Sharp teeth may suit meat; flatter teeth may suit plants.
Leg shape can suggest how it moved.
Horns, armor, and tail clubs may help protection.

comparePairs.title: Dinosaur vs Fossil

b.name: Fossil
points: may be bone, footprint, or eggshell

comparePairs.childConclusion: A fossil is not a living dinosaur; it is evidence.

comparePairs.title: Plant-eater vs Meat-eater

a.name: Plant-eater
points: mouth and teeth suited for plants

comparePairs.childConclusion: What an animal eats can shape its body.

clickTasks.title: Find: what evidence did dinosaurs leave?
clickTasks.wrongHint: Evidence is a clue left behind, not a walking dinosaur.
clickTasks.successCopy: Correct! Fossils and footprints can both be clues.

clickTasks.title: What might sharp teeth suggest?

options.label: May be suited for eating meat

wrongHints.leaf: Plant-eating teeth usually do not need to be so sharp.
wrongHints.toy: Body structures often relate to lifestyle.

clickTasks.successCopy: Right! Sharp teeth may relate to hunting or eating meat.

clickTasks.title: How does fossil research happen?
clickTasks.prompt: Tap the detective steps in order.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Find the clue first, then handle it carefully.
clickTasks.successCopy: You completed a paleontology detective workflow!

speakTemplates: I see ____, so it may mean _____.
A fossil is a clue left by _____.
Scientists do not just guess; they look at _____.
parentTips: Frame dinosaurs as natural history and evidence, not monster fighting.
Use teeth, feet, tail, and horns to guide observation.
If the child asks who is strongest, ask what helped each dinosaur survive.

intro: Dinosaurs lived a very long time ago.
We cannot meet them directly, but fossils and footprints let us become detectives.
keyFacts: Different dinosaurs had different body features.
Teeth, footprints, bones, and fossils provide clues.
Not all dinosaurs were fierce or meat-eating.
copy.explainPrompt: Can you use teeth, footprints, or body shape to guess how a dinosaur lived?

acceptanceCriteria: The child can name at least three dinosaur feature types.
The child knows fossils are evidence for learning about dinosaurs.
The child can distinguish dinosaurs from fossil evidence.
